content.title: About
content.content: Nougat with nuts is a confection made from whipped egg whites, sugar, honey, and roasted nuts (commonly walnuts, hazelnuts or almonds). It has a soft, slightly chewy texture and a flavor that blends sweet caramel notes with the aroma of toasted nuts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nougat has ancient roots: its ancestors were prepared in ancient Rome and Persia.
Traditionally, nuts are toasted to a golden hue before being folded into the nougat to release their flavor.
Different countries use different nuts: Italy often uses almonds, France prefers hazelnuts.
Nougat is frequently used as a filling for cakes, chocolates and ice cream.
Legend says the original nougat was created in the 13th century in the Arab town of Nuga.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and honey provide quick‑acting glucose, delivering an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Healthy fats from nuts
items.content: Nuts contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Nuts are rich in vitamin E, magnesium and selenium, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The nuts add plant‑based protein, useful for tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Nuts contribute fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: Nougat with nuts can trigger severe allergic reactions in people sensitive to nuts.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The large amount of sugar makes nougat calorie‑dense and may contribute to tooth decay if consumed frequently.

items.title: Honey content
items.content: Children under one year should not consume honey, so this confection is unsuitable for infants.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: Some manufacturers add artificial flavors or preservatives, which some consumers may wish to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Nougat with nuts can be enjoyed on its own, crumbled over pastries, used as a cake filling, or mixed into yogurt and ice cream. For a smoother texture, nuts can be finely chopped before incorporation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep nougat in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store it in the refrigerator to prevent sugar crystallisation. Discard if you notice mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Congee with egg is a traditional Asian comfort food consisting of a thick rice porridge cooked until the grains break down, with a boiled egg added for protein. Warm, soothing, and easy to digest, it is commonly served for breakfast or a light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Any rice variety can be used, but short‑grain rice is most common because it breaks down quickly.
In China congee is often topped with ginger, scallions, soy sauce, or pickled vegetables.
The egg is added at the end of cooking so the whites set while the yolk stays soft.
The dish is considered a “comfort food” and is frequently given to people recovering from illness.

items.title: Source of easily digestible carbs
items.content: Rice in congee provides quick‑release energy, helpful for recovery after sickness.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The egg supplies complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Both rice and egg deliver B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Gentle on the stomach
items.content: The soft texture makes it suitable for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high liquid content helps maintain the body’s water balance.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs should avoid this version of congee.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice porridge can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If soy sauce or broth is added, the sodium level may become high.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve congee hot, optionally topping with soy sauce, sliced scallions, ginger, or a drizzle of oil. The egg can be left whole, sliced, or stirred into the porridge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Refrigerate leftover congee in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore the desired consistency.

corn-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Corn, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Corn is a globally cultivated grain. Freshly cooked corn without added fat retains its natural sweet flavor and crisp texture. It is enjoyed as a side dish, in salads, soups, or as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most important agricultural crops and is used both for food and industry.
There are over 300 varieties of corn, differing in kernel color, taste, and maturity time.
Corn was domesticated more than 9,000 years ago in Mexico.
Sweet corn, commonly eaten boiled, contains more sugar than field corn used for animal feed.
Corn is rich in antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B5, and folate are involved in energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooked without added fat, corn contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to corn.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Enzyme content
items.content: Raw kernels contain enzymes that may cause stomach discomfort in sensitive individuals; cooking neutralizes them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn can be enjoyed hot right after cooking, added to salads, soups, chili, or grilled. It pairs well with lemon juice, fresh herbs, spices, and a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked corn in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze kernels in freezer bags for longer storage (up to 6 months). Reheat or serve cold before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans, cooked by boiling, are a popular side dish in restaurants. They have a tender flavor, a mildly sweet aroma, and a crisp texture when not overcooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and flavonoids.
They are used worldwide in salads, soups, and as a stand‑alone side.
The fiber content in cooked beans supports a healthy gut microbiome.
In the United States, green beans are often served with almonds or bacon in classic dishes.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Cooked green beans provide plant‑based protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Possible gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating and gas, especially if not chewed thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green beans can be served as a side, added to salads, soups, stews, or used in cold appetizers. They are often seasoned with salt, lemon juice, or lightly sautéed with garlic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked green beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in sealed bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned pineapple in syrup consists of bite‑size pieces of ripe pineapple that have been heat‑treated and sealed in a sweet sugar syrup. The product retains the characteristic aroma and sweetness of fresh pineapple while offering a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple is one of the few tropical fruits that is widely canned on an industrial scale.
The syrup is usually made from sugar and water, sometimes with a touch of citric acid to preserve the bright color.
Canned pineapple is a common ingredient in desserts, salads, and cocktails.
In the 19th century, canning pineapple became a popular way to ship this exotic fruit to markets without fresh supplies.
Pineapple in syrup can contain up to 20 % added sugar, making it more caloric than fresh fruit.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Pineapple provides a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: The enzyme bromelain aids protein digestion and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Source of manganese
items.content: Manganese is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and bone formation.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium in pineapple helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The syrup adds a significant amount of sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Pineapple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pineapple, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Presence of preservatives
items.content: Certain brands add preservatives such as potassium sorbate; those with sensitivities should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned pineapple can be enjoyed straight from the jar, added to fruit salads, yogurts, baked goods, smoothies, and ice cream. The syrup is often drained, but a small amount can be used as a sweetener.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the fruit refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold appears or an off‑odor develops.

rice-brown-with-soy-based-sauce-no-added.title: Brown Rice with Soy‑Based Sauce, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained from unrefined rice kernels. In this version it is served with a soy‑based sauce prepared without added fat, preserving the natural flavor and nutritional profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ layers, giving it more fiber and micronutrients than white rice.
Soy sauce is traditionally fermented from soybeans, wheat, salt and water, a process that can last from months to years.
The lack of added fat makes the dish low‑calorie while still providing protein and complex carbs.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.
Soy sauce naturally contains amino acids such as glutamate, which enhance the umami taste.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and cholesterol management.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs deliver sustained energy, beneficial for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function, nerve signaling, and bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Together, brown rice and soy sauce provide a complete set of amino acids useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products, including soy sauce.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Traditional soy sauce can be high in salt; choose a low‑sodium version if needed.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice hot, drizzled with the soy sauce. It can be added to salads, bowls, soups, or used as a side for vegetables and lean protein. Garnish with sliced green onions or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with sauce should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a starchy root vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. The NFS (Non‑Fungus‑Sensitive) variety is bred for higher resistance to fungal diseases and consistent tuber quality.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato belongs to the morning‑glory family, not the true potato family.
Tubers can have flesh colors ranging from white and yellow to orange, purple, and even blue.
In the United States sweet potato is classified as a vegetable, while in some countries it is considered a fruit because of its high sugar content.
The NFS variety was developed in the 1990s to reduce crop losses from Phytophthora infestations.
Orange‑fleshed sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than carrots.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Orange flesh provides provitamin A, which the body converts to vitamin A to support vision and immune function.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C enhances antioxidant protection and is essential for collagen synthesis.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index when cooked
items.content: Properly prepared sweet potato has a moderate impact on blood glucose, making it suitable for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance, while magnesium is important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some varieties contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation when consumed in excess.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, individuals may experience an allergy to sweet potato, resulting in skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Potential nitrate accumulation
items.content: Growing in overly fertilized soils can lead to nitrate buildup; thorough washing and proper cooking are recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet potatoes can be baked, boiled, steamed, fried, or mashed. They are used in soups, casseroles, salads, and desserts. For a softer texture, soak the tubers in cold water for 30 minutes before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sweet potatoes in a cool, dark, well‑ventilated area at 12‑15 °C. Do not refrigerate, as cold temperatures can alter flavor and texture. For long‑term storage, check regularly for soft spots or rot.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison sausage is a meat sausage made from ground venison, often seasoned with salt, spices, and sometimes a small amount of fat. Venison has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and is considered a leaner meat compared to beef or pork.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison contains less fat and fewer calories than most other meats.
In traditional northern cuisines, venison sausage was prepared in cold climates for long‑term storage.
Venison is rich in iron and zinc, making it a valuable source of these minerals.
Venison sausage is often smoked, giving it a distinctive aroma and extending shelf life.
In some European regions it is known as “sausage de cerf.”

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Venison provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Venison sausage typically contains less saturated fat than pork or beef sausages.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in venison is readily absorbed and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Vitamins B12, B6, and niacin support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Allergy to game meat
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to venison.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like most sausages, it can be high in sodium; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Risk of contamination
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth.

items.title: Higher cost
items.content: Venison is usually more expensive than other meats, which may limit frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison sausage can be enjoyed cold as a snack, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, pastas, or pan‑fried. It pairs well with mustard, cranberry sauce, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store venison sausage in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage freeze it at –18 °C; it will retain quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Yeast are single‑cell fungi used in cooking, brewing, and baking for fermentation. The most common type is the brewer’s yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. They convert sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, making dough rise and giving beverages their alcoholic character.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yeast have been used by humans for more than 7,000 years; the earliest archaeological evidence comes from ancient Egypt.
There are over 1,500 yeast species, but only a few dozen are employed in food production.
Yeast can survive extreme conditions, tolerating high sugar, salt, and alcohol concentrations.
In 1928, Elie Willyard discovered yeast as a model organism for genetics, paving the way for modern molecular biology.
Dry yeast is sold as granules, allowing it to stay active for up to two years at room temperature.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast provide thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folate, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Dry yeast contains about 40 % protein, including all essential amino acids, making it a valuable addition to vegetarian diets.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Yeast are a source of iron, zinc, magnesium, and selenium, important for immunity and metabolic processes.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Beta‑glucans in yeast promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria and may improve digestive health.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption of yeast powder can reduce total cholesterol and LDL levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to yeast, ranging from skin rashes to swelling and breathing difficulties.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Yeast are rich in purines, which can increase uric acid production and may be problematic for people with gout.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Dry yeast is often fortified with salt; those limiting sodium should choose unsalted varieties.

items.title: Excessive intake
items.content: Large amounts can cause gastrointestinal upset, such as gas, bloating, and diarrhea.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Yeast can be added to bread, rolls, and pizza dough, sprinkled over finished dishes, used in sauces and soups, or dissolved in water or juice as a nutritious drink. Dry yeast is typically sold as a powder, making it easy to store and dose.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry yeast in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. After opening, keep it in the refrigerator, where it remains active for up to 12 months. Discard yeast that smells moldy or feels damp.
